In the vast vacuum of space, conventional sound as humans experience it does not exist, because sound requires a medium of vibrating particles to travel and space is largely empty [d1][d3]. As stated by a university physics source, "sound does not travel at all in space" since "the vacuum of outer space has essentially zero air" to vibrate [d3]. However, space is not entirely empty: in gas-rich regions such as galaxy clusters, true low-frequency sound waves (pressure waves) can propagate through the thin gas [d4][d6][d7]. For example, NASA detected actual sound waves rippling through the hot gas surrounding the black hole at the center of the Perseus galaxy cluster, though these waves are 57 octaves below middle C — far beyond human hearing [d2][d4]. Scientists use a technique called sonification to convert non-auditory space data (such as plasma waves or electromagnetic signals) into audible sound for analysis, but these are not sound waves traveling through space itself [d5][d9].
